Pelethites
PEL-eth-ites
n. pl.
A body of foreign soldiers forming David’s personal guard, always named with the Cherethites. The names are commonly connected with the Philistines and the Cretans — men from the coast David had lived among in exile, who became the king’s most trusted troops and the only force that stayed loyal through two rebellions.

Biblical Definition

The Pelethites appear only in company with the Cherethites, and always in the same office: Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over both the Cherethites and the Pelethites (2 Samuel 8:18), a note repeated at 2 Samuel 20:23 and 1 Chronicles 18:17. They are the royal bodyguard, foreigners in an Israelite army, and their record is remarkable. On the day David fled Jerusalem before Absalom, all the Cherethites, and all the Pelethites, and all the Gittites, six hundred men which came after him from Gath, passed on before the king (2 Samuel 15:18) — the household troops went out with a king who had lost his capital, while Israel’s own counsellor Ahithophel went over to the usurper. When Sheba the son of Bichri raised the second revolt, there went out after him Joab’s men, and the Cherethites, and the Pelethites, and all the mighty men (2 Samuel 20:7). And at the end, when Adonijah had proclaimed himself king, it was Zadok, Nathan, Benaiah, and the Cherethites and Pelethites who brought Solomon down to Gihon and set him on the throne (1 Kings 1:38). Three crises of the house of David, and the foreign guard is on the right side of all three.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 has no PELETHITE entry. The word appears seven times in Scripture and never alone; its meaning is disputed, but the office — the king’s personal guard under Benaiah — is perfectly clear from the contexts.

expand to see more

PELETHITES, n. pl. — A company of David’s guard, always mentioned with the Cherethites, and commanded by Benaiah the son of Jehoiada.

The name is often connected with the Hebrew for Philistine, as Cherethite is with Crete; both would then denote coastland mercenaries.

They are named seven times, all in 2 Samuel, 1 Kings 1, and 1 Chronicles 18 — and never separately from the Cherethites.

An alternative older explanation derives the two names from words for executioners and couriers, the two functions of a royal guard.

Webster 1828 does not carry the term; the office is defined by 2 Samuel 8:18, 15:18, 20:7, 20:23, and 1 Kings 1:38.

Key Scripture

2 Samuel 8:18 — "And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over both the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and David’s sons were chief rulers."

2 Samuel 15:18 — "And all his servants passed on beside him; and all the Cherethites, and all the Pelethites, and all the Gittites, six hundred men which came after him from Gath, passed on before the king."

2 Samuel 20:7 — "And there went out after him Joab’s men, and the Cherethites, and the Pelethites, and all the mighty men: and they went out of Jerusalem, to pursue after Sheba the son of Bichri."

2 Samuel 20:23 — "Now Joab was over all the host of Israel: and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and over the Pelethites:"

1 Chronicles 18:17 — "And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and the sons of David were chief about the king."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that covenant loyalty is not produced by blood or nationality, and that the men nearest a king in his fall are rarely the men who have most to gain.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What deserves recovery is the pattern of loyalty in 2 Samuel 15. David goes up the ascent of Olivet weeping, barefoot, his head covered, while the hearts of the men of Israel go after Absalom. Who stays? A guard of Cherethites and Pelethites, six hundred Gittites newly come from Gath under Ittai, Zadok and Abiathar with the ark, and Hushai the Archite. Almost none of them are men with a natural stake in the house of David. Ahithophel, who had every stake, defected. The pattern recurs whenever a good work is under pressure, and any pastor who has watched a church go through a hard season will recognize it: the people who stay are frequently not the ones the register would have predicted.

The second point is a matter of order rather than sentiment. These were foreigners, and they were placed under an Israelite captain, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, who was himself a priest’s son and one of the three mighty men. They are never given command; they are given a charge under authority. Scripture consistently welcomes the stranger into the service of the covenant people while keeping the offices ordered, and both halves of that are needed. A body that cannot receive outsiders becomes a clan; a body that receives them without order becomes something other than itself. David did both rightly, and on the day his own son took his throne it was the foreigners under Benaiah who brought Solomon to Gihon.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Pelethi (H6432), Pelethite, always paired with Kerethi (H3774), Cherethite; both names are usually traced to the coastland peoples of Philistia and Crete.

expand to see more

Hebrew Pelethi (H6432) — Pelethite; a courier or runner, on one derivation, from a root meaning to be swift.

Hebrew Kerethi (H3774) — Cherethite; connected with Crete, and used in parallel with Philistines at Zephaniah 2:5.

Hebrew Pelishti (H6430) — Philistine; the likely cognate behind Pelethi.

Hebrew Benayahu (H1141) — Benaiah, the LORD hath built; their captain, and afterward Solomon’s commander-in-chief.

Hebrew mishmereth — a charge, a watch; the standing term for a guard’s appointed duty.

Usage

"Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over both the Cherethites and the Pelethites (2 Samuel 8:18) — the guard under an Israelite captain."

"All the Cherethites, and all the Pelethites… passed on before the king (2 Samuel 15:18) — loyalty on the day of flight."

"Benaiah… was over the Cherethites and over the Pelethites (2 Samuel 20:23) — the office kept through both rebellions."
